summary: Supply the A₁, the B₁ and the C₁ and the Matrix addition and subtraction calculator solves for size. It suits a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Matrix addition and subtraction calculator work?
sections.html:
The Matrix addition and subtraction calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports size in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the operation, number of rows and number of columns); then you type in the A₁ (First matrix entries), the A₁ (First matrix entries), the A₁ (First matrix entries) and the A₁ (First matrix entries).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Matrix addition and subtraction calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Size=number of columns + 10 × number of rows
C₁₁=(operation, A₁, X₁)
C₂₁=(operation, B₁, Y₁)
C₃₁=(operation, C₁, Z₁)
C₄₁=(operation, D₁, U₁)
C₁₂=(operation, A₂, X₂)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Operation set to Addition, Number of rows set to 2 and Number of columns set to 2. Straight away the calculator returns Size = 22.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Size = 22 should be roughly the size you expected from Operation set to Addition and Number of rows set to 2.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Matrix addition and subtraction calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the A₁, the B₁ and the C₁ — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Matrix addition and subtraction calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns size, derived from the A₁, the B₁ and the C₁. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Matrix addition and subtraction calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the A₁, the B₁ and the C₁, which is 83 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Size = 22. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Matrix addition and subtraction calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
